notes.front: What is static testing?
notes.back: “A test approach that does not involve the execution of a test item.”
notes.explanation: Nothing is run: the test item is examined instead.
notes.example: Like proof-reading a recipe for missing steps, rather than cooking it to see what goes wrong.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “static testing”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A test approach that does not involve the execution of a test item.

notes.front: What is dynamic testing?
notes.back: “A test approach that involves test execution of a test item.”
notes.explanation: It is the counterpart of static testing: the item is actually run.
notes.example: Like cooking the recipe and tasting the result.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “dynamic testing”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A test approach that involves test execution of a test item.

notes.front: What is static analysis?
notes.back: “The automated process of evaluating a component or system without executing it, based on its form, structure, content, or documentation.”
notes.explanation: The key word is “automated”: a tool does the evaluating, and nothing is run.
notes.example: Like a grammar checker flagging a sentence with no verb, but for program code.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “static analysis”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: The automated process of evaluating a component or system without executing it, based on its form, structure, content, or documentation.

notes.front: What is a review?
notes.back: “A type of static testing in which the quality of a work product or process is evaluated by individuals.”
notes.explanation: Where static analysis relies on tools, a review relies on people judging quality.
notes.example: Like colleagues reading a draft contract and marking unclear clauses.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “review”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A type of static testing in which the quality of a work product or process is evaluated by individuals.

notes.front: What is an anomaly?
notes.back: “A condition that deviates from expectation.”
notes.explanation: The definition says nothing about who is at fault; it only records that something is not as expected.
notes.example: Like a reviewer noticing that a screen mock-up shows four menu items where the text mentions five.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “anomaly”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A condition that deviates from expectation.

notes.front: In a review, what is the manager’s role?
notes.back: To choose what gets reviewed, and to supply the resources for it, such as people and time.
notes.explanation: The manager controls both the choice of work product and the resources for reviewing it.
notes.example: Like a head of department who decides the new policy draft will be reviewed and frees two staff for a day to do it.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.3 “Roles and Responsibilities in Reviews”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a review, what is the author’s role?
notes.back: To create the work product under review, and to fix it.
notes.explanation: The person who wrote it is also the one who acts on the findings.
notes.example: Like the analyst who wrote a requirements document and later corrects it after reviewers’ comments.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.3 “Roles and Responsibilities in Reviews”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a review, what is the moderator’s role, and what else is the moderator called?
notes.back: To ensure review meetings run effectively (mediation, time management, a safe environment to speak freely); also called the facilitator.
notes.explanation: The role is about how the meeting runs, not about the content being reviewed.
notes.example: Like a chairperson who keeps a heated design meeting to time and makes sure the quietest person gets heard.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.3 “Roles and Responsibilities in Reviews”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a review, what is the scribe’s role, and what else is the scribe called?
notes.back: To gather all reviewers’ anomalies and record what the review meeting produces, such as decisions and newly found anomalies; also called the recorder.
notes.explanation: The scribe is the review’s record-keeper, both for reviewers’ findings and for the meeting.
notes.example: Like the club secretary who gathers members’ written comments and minutes what the committee decides.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.3 “Roles and Responsibilities in Reviews”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a review, what is the reviewer’s role, and who can be one?
notes.back: To do the reviewing; a reviewer can be a project member, a subject matter expert or any other stakeholder.
notes.explanation: The syllabus keeps the role open, so reviewers can bring very different viewpoints.
notes.example: Like asking a nurse, as well as developers, to read the specification for a ward-rostering app.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.3 “Roles and Responsibilities in Reviews”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a review, what is the review leader’s role?
notes.back: To own the review as a whole, for example choosing the participants and arranging its time and place.
notes.explanation: The review leader runs the review as a whole, while the moderator looks after the meetings themselves.
notes.example: Like the organiser who picks the panel, books the room and sets the date for a design review.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.3 “Roles and Responsibilities in Reviews”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a formal review?
notes.back: “A review that follows a defined process with a formally documented output.”
notes.explanation: Two things make it formal: a defined process, and documented results.
notes.example: Like a planning committee that follows set procedures and publishes minutes of its decision.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “formal review”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A review that follows a defined process with a formally documented output.

notes.front: What is an informal review?
notes.back: “A type of review that does not follow a defined process and has no formally documented output.”
notes.explanation: It lacks both features that make a review formal.
notes.example: Like asking the colleague at the next desk to glance over an email before you send it.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “informal review”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A type of review that does not follow a defined process and has no formally documented output.

notes.front: What is a walkthrough?
notes.back: A formal review in which an author leads members through a work product while they ask questions and make comments.
notes.explanation: The author is in the driving seat, guiding the others through the work.
notes.example: Like an architect talking a client through the plans room by room while the client asks questions.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “walkthrough”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A type of formal review in which an author leads members of the review through a work product and the members ask questions and make comments.

notes.front: What is a technical review?
notes.back: “A formal review by technical experts that examine the quality of a work product and identify discrepancies from specifications and standards.”
notes.explanation: The reviewers’ technical expertise is what defines it.
notes.example: Like structural engineers checking a bridge design against the building codes.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “technical review”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A formal review by technical experts that examine the quality of a work product and identify discrepancies from specifications and standards.

notes.front: What is an inspection?
notes.back: A formal review using defined team roles and measurement to identify defects in a work product, and to improve the review and development processes.
notes.explanation: Measurement is the distinctive part: the data collected feeds back into improving the processes.
notes.example: Like an aircraft maintenance check with fixed roles and a logged checklist, whose records are also used to improve future checks.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “inspection”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A type of formal review that uses defined team roles and measurement to identify defects in a work product, and improve the review process and the software development process.

notes.front: In static testing, what are the two ways work products are evaluated?
notes.back: By people examining them by hand (as in reviews) or by a tool (as in static analysis).
notes.explanation: Reviews rely on people; static analysis relies on tools.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1 “Static Testing Basics”, p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two test objectives of static testing?
notes.back: Any two of: improving quality; detecting defects; assessing characteristics such as readability, completeness, correctness, testability and consistency.
notes.explanation: Static testing is not only about finding defects; it also judges how good a work product is.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1 “Static Testing Basics”, p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two characteristics of a work product that static testing can assess?
notes.back: Any two of: readability, completeness, correctness, testability, consistency.
notes.explanation: The syllabus introduces these with “like”, so the list is not closed.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1 “Static Testing Basics”, p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester reads a new data-retention policy document and marks sentences that contradict each other. Is this static or dynamic testing?
notes.back: Static testing
notes.choices:
A) Static testing
B) Dynamic testing
C) Neither; documents cannot be tested
notes.choicesExplained: B: nothing is being executed. C: static testing examines work products such as documents.
notes.explanation: Evaluating a work product by examination, without running anything, is static testing.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1 “Static Testing Basics”, p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Can static testing be used for verification, for validation, or both?
notes.back: Both.
notes.explanation: Reviewing a document can check it is built right and that it describes the right thing.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1 “Static Testing Basics”, p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How can review techniques be applied to user stories?
notes.back: To check that each story is complete, easy to understand and carries acceptance criteria that can be tested.
notes.explanation: Testable acceptance criteria are named explicitly as something a story should include.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1 “Static Testing Basics”, p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When testers take part in backlog refinement or collaborative story writing, how do they help improve the proposed user stories?
notes.back: Through well-aimed questions that probe the stories, push back on them and make them better.
notes.explanation: Questions from a tester’s angle expose gaps that the story’s writers may not see.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1 “Static Testing Basics”, p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why does static analysis often need less effort than dynamic testing?
notes.back: No test cases are needed, and tools are typically used.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says “often”: static analysis can find problems before dynamic testing with less effort.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1 “Static Testing Basics”, p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Into what kind of framework is static analysis often incorporated?
notes.back: CI frameworks.
notes.explanation: This links static analysis to the CI practice described under DevOps.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1 “Static Testing Basics”, p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team adds a code-checking tool to its CI pipeline, and it flags problems in every commit before any tests are run. Which advantage of static analysis does this show?
notes.back: It can find problems before dynamic testing, often with less effort
notes.choices:
A) It can find problems before dynamic testing, often with less effort
B) It replaces the need for dynamic testing
C) It measures performance efficiency
notes.choicesExplained: B: static and dynamic testing complement each other; some defects can only be found dynamically. C: characteristics that depend on running code are measured by dynamic testing.
notes.explanation: No test cases are needed and a tool does the work, so issues surface early and cheaply.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1 “Static Testing Basics”, p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides detecting specific code defects, what two things is static analysis also used to evaluate?
notes.back: Maintainability and security.
notes.explanation: Both can be judged from how the code is written, without running it.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1 “Static Testing Basics”, p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Beyond code checkers, what two other examples of static analysis tools does the syllabus give?
notes.back: Spelling checkers and readability tools.
notes.explanation: They too evaluate a work product automatically without executing anything.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1 “Static Testing Basics”, p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which work products can be examined using static testing?
notes.back: Almost any work product.
notes.explanation: The syllabus’s examples range from code and test cases to contracts and models.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.1 “Work Products Examinable by Static Testing”, p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two examples of work products that static testing can examine?
notes.back: Any two of, among others: requirement specifications, source code, test plans, test cases, backlog items, test charters, project documents, contracts, models.
notes.explanation: The syllabus gives these as examples; almost any work product qualifies.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.1 “Work Products Examinable by Static Testing”, p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A supplier contract for a new payroll system is about to be signed. Can it be examined by static testing?
notes.back: Yes. Contracts are among the work products the syllabus lists as examinable by static testing.
notes.explanation: Anything that can be read and understood can be reviewed, and contracts are named explicitly.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.1 “Work Products Examinable by Static Testing”, p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does a work product need in order to be the subject of a review?
notes.back: It must be something that can be read and understood.
notes.explanation: A review relies on people, so anything people can make sense of qualifies.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.1 “Work Products Examinable by Static Testing”, p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does a work product need before static analysis can check it?
notes.back: A structure it can be checked against, such as models, code, or text with a formal syntax.
notes.explanation: A tool needs rules to check against, which free-form material does not provide.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.1 “Work Products Examinable by Static Testing”, p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team has free-form notes from a brainstorming session about a new app. Can they be reviewed, analysed by static analysis, or both?
notes.back: Reviewed, but not easily analysed by static analysis
notes.choices:
A) Reviewed, but not easily analysed by static analysis
B) Analysed by static analysis, but not reviewed
C) Neither
notes.choicesExplained: B: static analysis needs a structure to check against, which free notes lack, while anything readable can be reviewed. C: readable notes can always be reviewed.
notes.explanation: Review needs only readability; static analysis needs a structure such as code or formal syntax.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.1 “Work Products Examinable by Static Testing”, p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which work products are not appropriate for static testing?
notes.back: Ones people can hardly interpret and tools must not examine, such as a supplier’s compiled program whose licence forbids analysing it.
notes.explanation: If people cannot read it and tools may not examine it, neither form of static testing is open.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.1 “Work Products Examinable by Static Testing”, p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In which phases of the SDLC can static testing detect defects?
notes.back: The earliest phases, fulfilling the principle of early testing.
notes.explanation: The syllabus ties this to the principle of early testing.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.2 “Value of Static Testing”, p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Can static testing find defects that dynamic testing cannot?
notes.back: Yes, for example defects in work products that cannot be executed.
notes.explanation: Dynamic testing can only reach what runs; static testing reaches everything that can be examined.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.2 “Value of Static Testing”, p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides finding defects, what does static testing provide for work products?
notes.back: The ability to evaluate their quality and to build confidence in them.
notes.explanation: A reviewed document is one people can rely on more.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.2 “Value of Static Testing”, p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: By verifying the documented requirements, what can stakeholders make sure of?
notes.back: That the requirements describe their actual needs.
notes.explanation: Reading the requirements lets stakeholders spot where what is written differs from what they want.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.2 “Value of Static Testing”, p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Because static testing can be done early, what can it create among stakeholders?
notes.back: A shared understanding, with improved communication between them.
notes.explanation: This is why the syllabus recommends involving a wide variety of stakeholders in static testing.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.2 “Value of Static Testing”, p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team plans to review a new benefits-claim form with only its two developers. What does the syllabus recommend instead?
notes.back: Involving a wide variety of stakeholders, which builds shared understanding and improves communication.
notes.explanation: The syllabus links wide involvement to shared understanding and better communication.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.2 “Value of Static Testing”, p. 33
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is usually the result of detecting certain code defects with static analysis rather than dynamic testing?
notes.back: Usually fewer defects left in the code, and less development effort in total.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says static analysis finds these defects more efficiently, “usually” with this result.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.2 “Value of Static Testing”, p. 34
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Reviews can be costly. Why are overall project costs usually much lower with them than without?
notes.back: Less time and effort is needed to fix defects later in the project.
notes.explanation: The cost of reviewing is outweighed by the rework it avoids; the syllabus says “usually”.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.2 “Value of Static Testing”, p. 34
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A finance director wants to cancel all document reviews to save the week of staff time they take on each project. What does the syllabus say about the likely effect on overall cost?
notes.back: Costs will usually be higher, because more time goes on fixing defects later
notes.choices:
A) Costs will usually be higher, because more time goes on fixing defects later
B) Costs will fall by exactly the review time saved
C) Costs will not change
notes.choicesExplained: B: this ignores the later fixing effort that reviews prevent. C: the syllabus says overall costs are usually much lower with reviews than without.
notes.explanation: Reviews cost effort, but projects without them usually spend more on later defect fixing.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.2 “Value of Static Testing”, p. 34
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How do static testing and dynamic testing relate to each other?
notes.back: They complement each other, with similar objectives such as supporting the detection of defects.
notes.explanation: Each can find defect types the other cannot, so neither replaces the other.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.3 “Differences between Static Testing and Dynamic Testing”, p. 34
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How do static and dynamic testing differ in the way they reach defects?
notes.back: Static testing finds defects directly; dynamic testing causes failures, and the defects behind them are found by later analysis.
notes.explanation: Dynamic testing sees symptoms first; static testing sees the cause itself.
notes.contrast: Defect found directly versus failure first, then analysis.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.3 “Differences between Static Testing and Dynamic Testing”, p. 34
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which may more easily detect defects on code paths that are rarely executed or hard to reach: static or dynamic testing?
notes.back: Static testing.
notes.explanation: Examining code does not depend on driving execution down an awkward path.
notes.contrast: Static testing can read awkward paths directly; dynamic testing has to drive execution down them.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.3 “Differences between Static Testing and Dynamic Testing”, p. 34
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which kind of testing can examine work products that cannot be run, and which needs ones that can?
notes.back: Static testing works on non-executable work products too; dynamic testing needs something that can run.
notes.explanation: Dynamic testing needs something to run; static testing does not.
notes.contrast: Anything readable versus only what can run.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.3 “Differences between Static Testing and Dynamic Testing”, p. 34
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which kind of testing measures quality characteristics that depend on executing code, and which measures those that do not?
notes.back: Dynamic testing measures those that depend on running code (such as performance efficiency); static testing those that do not (such as maintainability).
notes.explanation: Some qualities only appear when code runs; others can be judged from the code itself.
notes.contrast: Qualities of running behaviour versus qualities of the code as written.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.3 “Differences between Static Testing and Dynamic Testing”, p. 34
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Can static and dynamic testing each find every type of defect?
notes.back: No. Some defect types can only be found by static testing, and some only by dynamic testing.
notes.explanation: This is why the two are used together rather than choosing one.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.3 “Differences between Static Testing and Dynamic Testing”, p. 34
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team wants to know how many requests per second its new search service can handle. Static or dynamic testing?
notes.back: Dynamic testing
notes.choices:
A) Dynamic testing
B) Static testing
C) Either works equally well
notes.choicesExplained: B: throughput depends on running the code, which static testing does not do. C: only dynamic testing can measure characteristics that depend on execution.
notes.explanation: Performance efficiency depends on executing code, which is dynamic testing’s territory.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.3 “Differences between Static Testing and Dynamic Testing”, p. 34
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team wants to judge how easy its billing code will be for others to change in future. Static or dynamic testing?
notes.back: Static testing
notes.choices:
A) Static testing
B) Dynamic testing
C) Neither
notes.choicesExplained: B: maintainability does not depend on executing the code. C: the syllabus names maintainability as something static testing can measure.
notes.explanation: Maintainability can be judged from the code as written, without running it.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.3 “Differences between Static Testing and Dynamic Testing”, p. 34
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two types of defect that are typically easier or cheaper to find through static testing?
notes.back: Any two of: requirement defects; design defects; certain coding defects; deviations from standards; incorrect interface specifications; some security vulnerabilities; test-basis coverage gaps.
notes.explanation: All seven can be seen in documents or code without running anything.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.3 “Differences between Static Testing and Dynamic Testing”, p. 34
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a review, one requirement says passwords must be at least 8 characters and another says at least 12. What type of defect has static testing found?
notes.back: A defect in the requirements.
notes.explanation: Contradictions between requirements are a typical defect that static testing finds easily.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.3 “Differences between Static Testing and Dynamic Testing”, p. 34
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A design review finds that a single module handles screens, business rules and data storage all at once. What type of defect is this?
notes.back: A design defect.
notes.explanation: Poorly structured designs can be spotted on paper, before they are built.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.3 “Differences between Static Testing and Dynamic Testing”, p. 34
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A static analysis tool reports a function with forty nested conditions, far beyond the team’s limit for complexity. What type of defect is this?
notes.back: A coding defect (excessive code complexity).
notes.explanation: Certain coding defects like this are easier to find by examining code than by running it.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.3 “Differences between Static Testing and Dynamic Testing”, p. 34
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The team’s coding standard bans unexplained numeric constants, but a reviewer finds 86400 typed directly into the code in several places. What type of defect is this?
notes.back: A deviation from standards.
notes.explanation: Checking code against an agreed standard is a static activity.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.3 “Differences between Static Testing and Dynamic Testing”, p. 34
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: One specification says a pricing service returns amounts in pence; the specification of the program calling it expects pounds. What type of defect has a review found?
notes.back: An incorrect interface specification.
notes.explanation: Two sides of an interface that disagree on paper will fail when joined.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.3 “Differences between Static Testing and Dynamic Testing”, p. 34
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A code scan finds that user input is copied into a fixed-size memory area with no length check. Which type of defect typically found by static testing is this?
notes.back: A security vulnerability.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says specific types of security vulnerability are easier to find through static testing.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.3 “Differences between Static Testing and Dynamic Testing”, p. 34
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A review of the test cases shows that the requirement “lock the account after five failed logins” has no test traced to it. What type of defect is this?
notes.back: A gap in test basis coverage.
notes.explanation: Missing coverage of the test basis can be seen by comparing documents, without running tests.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.1.3 “Differences between Static Testing and Dynamic Testing”, p. 34
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does early and frequent stakeholder feedback allow to be communicated early?
notes.back: Potential quality problems.
notes.explanation: The benefit is about timing: concerns reach the team early.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.1 “Benefits of Early and Frequent Stakeholder Feedback”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What can frequent stakeholder feedback do for requirements throughout the SDLC?
notes.back: Prevent misunderstandings, and make sure requirement changes are understood and implemented earlier.
notes.explanation: Regular contact keeps the team’s picture of the requirements current.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.1 “Benefits of Early and Frequent Stakeholder Feedback”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Frequent stakeholder feedback lets the development team focus on which features?
notes.back: Those that give stakeholders the most value and do most to address the identified risks.
notes.explanation: Better understanding of what is being built shows the team where effort matters most.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.1 “Benefits of Early and Frequent Stakeholder Feedback”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team shows a ticket-booking prototype to the client every fortnight, and in week four learns that group bookings matter more than seat maps. Which benefit of frequent feedback is this?
notes.back: Focusing on the features that deliver the most value
notes.choices:
A) Focusing on the features that deliver the most value
B) Removing the need for testing
C) Avoiding any change to requirements
notes.choicesExplained: B: feedback improves understanding; it does not replace testing. C: feedback helps changes be understood and made earlier; it does not stop them.
notes.explanation: Early feedback redirected effort to what the stakeholder values most.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.1 “Benefits of Early and Frequent Stakeholder Feedback”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: If stakeholders are little involved during the SDLC, what might happen to the product?
notes.back: It may not match what the stakeholder first pictured, or pictures now.
notes.explanation: Without their input, the team builds on its own guesses about what is wanted.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.1 “Benefits of Early and Frequent Stakeholder Feedback”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What can failing to deliver what the stakeholder wants lead to?
notes.back: Costly rework, missed deadlines and blame games, and possibly complete project failure.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says it “might even” end the project, keeping that outcome as a possibility.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.1 “Benefits of Early and Frequent Stakeholder Feedback”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the international review standard that the syllabus cites define?
notes.back: A generic review process: a framework with structure but room to be adapted to each situation.
notes.explanation: One framework can serve very different reviews by being tailored.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.2 “Review Process Activities”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What changes in the review process when the required review is more formal?
notes.back: More of the tasks listed for each activity have to be carried out.
notes.explanation: Formality scales the amount of process, not the list of activities.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.2 “Review Process Activities”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What can be done when a work product is too large for a single review?
notes.back: The review process can be invoked several times to cover the whole work product.
notes.explanation: Splitting keeps each review manageable while still covering everything.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.2 “Review Process Activities”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are the five activities of the review process, in order?
notes.back: Planning, review initiation, individual review, communication and analysis, fixing and reporting.
notes.explanation: Preparation comes first, then finding anomalies, then deciding on them, then acting on them.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.2 “Review Process Activities”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the review process, individual review is followed by {{c1::communication and analysis}}.
notes.explanation: Anomalies found alone are then discussed and decided on together.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.2 “Review Process Activities”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the review process, planning is followed by {{c1::review initiation}}.
notes.explanation: Once scope is set, everyone must be made ready before reviewing starts.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.2 “Review Process Activities”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Reviewers have each read a design document on their own and logged their anomalies. Which review activity comes next?
notes.back: Communication and analysis
notes.choices:
A) Communication and analysis
B) Review initiation
C) Planning
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: both come before individual review, which has just finished.
notes.explanation: After individual review, the logged anomalies are analysed and discussed.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.2 “Review Process Activities”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is defined during the planning of a review?
notes.back: Its scope: purpose, work product, quality characteristics, focus areas, exit criteria, supporting information, effort and timeframes.
notes.explanation: Everything later activities depend on is settled here first.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.2 “Review Process Activities”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Before a review, a lead writes down which chapters will be reviewed, that the focus is security, and that the review must finish by Friday. Which review activity is this?
notes.back: Planning
notes.choices:
A) Planning
B) Individual review
C) Fixing and reporting
notes.choicesExplained: B: nobody is reviewing yet. C: nothing has been found to fix or report.
notes.explanation: Setting the work product, focus areas and timeframe is part of defining the review’s scope in planning.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.2 “Review Process Activities”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the goal of review initiation?
notes.back: To get every person and every item ready before reviewing begins.
notes.explanation: Initiation is about the readiness of people and material alike.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.2 “Review Process Activities”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: During review initiation, what should every participant have?
notes.back: Access to the work product, an understanding of their role and responsibilities, and everything needed to perform the review.
notes.explanation: These three together mean each person can start reviewing without delay.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.2 “Review Process Activities”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: On the day reviewing should start, two reviewers find they cannot open the shared document and one does not know what they are meant to check. Which review activity was done poorly?
notes.back: Review initiation
notes.choices:
A) Review initiation
B) Communication and analysis
C) Fixing and reporting
notes.choicesExplained: B: that activity comes after reviewing. C: nothing has been found yet.
notes.explanation: Initiation should ensure everyone has access and understands their role.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.2 “Review Process Activities”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In individual review, what does each reviewer identify?
notes.back: Anomalies, recommendations and questions, all of which they log.
notes.explanation: The log is what the next activity, communication and analysis, works through.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.2 “Review Process Activities”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How do reviewers carry out individual review?
notes.back: By applying one or more review techniques, such as checklist-based or scenario-based reviewing.
notes.explanation: The syllabus names checklist-based and scenario-based reviewing as examples.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.2 “Review Process Activities”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A reviewer works alone through a test plan using a checklist and notes three anomalies and one question. Which review activity is she performing?
notes.back: Individual review
notes.choices:
A) Individual review
B) Review initiation
C) Communication and analysis
notes.choicesExplained: B: initiation prepares participants; it does not involve reviewing. C: that activity involves discussing anomalies with others, not working alone.
notes.explanation: Applying a technique alone and logging anomalies and questions is individual review.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.2 “Review Process Activities”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why must all anomalies found in a review be analysed and discussed?
notes.back: Because they are not necessarily defects.
notes.explanation: Something unexpected may still be correct, so each needs a decision.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.2 “Review Process Activities”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A reviewer logs that a report omits weekend figures. In discussion, the author shows the business asked for weekdays only. What was the logged item?
notes.back: An anomaly that turned out not to be a defect
notes.choices:
A) An anomaly that turned out not to be a defect
B) A defect, because every anomaly is a defect
C) A failure
notes.choicesExplained: B: the syllabus says review anomalies are not necessarily defects. C: a failure happens when software runs; this is a document review.
notes.explanation: It deviated from the reviewer’s expectation, but analysis showed it was correct.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.2 “Review Process Activities”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In communication and analysis, what is decided for every anomaly?
notes.back: Its status, its ownership and the actions required.
notes.explanation: Each anomaly leaves the discussion with a clear outcome and someone responsible.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.2 “Review Process Activities”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Where is communication and analysis typically done, and what else is decided there?
notes.back: In a review meeting, where participants also decide the reviewed work product’s quality level and the follow-up actions.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says “typically”: a meeting is usual but not the only way.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.2 “Review Process Activities”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What may be needed to complete the actions agreed in communication and analysis?
notes.back: A follow-up review.
notes.explanation: Some actions are big enough that their results need reviewing in turn.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.2 “Review Process Activities”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a meeting, the team goes through 30 logged anomalies, marking each as accepted or rejected, naming an owner and agreeing what to do. Which review activity is this?
notes.back: Communication and analysis
notes.choices:
A) Communication and analysis
B) Individual review
C) Planning
notes.choicesExplained: B: individual review is done alone and produces the log. C: planning sets scope before any anomalies exist.
notes.explanation: Deciding status, ownership and actions for each anomaly is communication and analysis.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.2 “Review Process Activities”, p. 35
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In fixing and reporting, what should be created for every defect, and why?
notes.back: A defect report for each defect, so the corrective work can be tracked.
notes.explanation: A written record makes sure each fix is tracked to completion.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.2 “Review Process Activities”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When can the reviewed work product be accepted?
notes.back: Once the exit criteria are reached; the review results are then reported.
notes.explanation: Acceptance depends on the criteria set during planning being met.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.2 “Review Process Activities”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The author has corrected the confirmed defects, each tracked through its own defect report, the exit criteria are met, and a summary is sent to the project board. Which review activity is this?
notes.back: Fixing and reporting
notes.choices:
A) Fixing and reporting
B) Review initiation
C) Individual review
notes.choicesExplained: B: initiation happens before any reviewing. C: individual review finds anomalies; it does not fix them or report results.
notes.explanation: Tracking fixes, accepting at the exit criteria and reporting results make up the final activity.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.2 “Review Process Activities”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Can one stakeholder take on more than one review role?
notes.back: Yes. Stakeholders may take on several roles.
notes.explanation: One person can hold two roles, say reviewer and scribe, although inspections bar the author from some of them.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.3 “Roles and Responsibilities in Reviews”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Are the six principal review roles the only roles possible?
notes.back: No. Other, more detailed roles are possible, as the review standard the syllabus cites describes.
notes.explanation: The syllabus covers only the principal roles.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.3 “Roles and Responsibilities in Reviews”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Who in a review decides that the new tariff specification will be reviewed and gives three staff two days for it?
notes.back: The manager
notes.choices:
A) The manager
B) The review leader
C) The moderator
notes.choicesExplained: B: the review leader organises who is involved and when, but the syllabus gives deciding what is reviewed and providing resources to the manager. C: the moderator runs the meetings.
notes.explanation: Deciding what to review and providing staff and time is the manager’s responsibility.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.3 “Roles and Responsibilities in Reviews”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: After the review, who updates the user guide to fix the confirmed defects?
notes.back: The author
notes.choices:
A) The author
B) The scribe
C) The manager
notes.choicesExplained: B: the scribe records anomalies and decisions but does not fix the work product. C: the manager provides resources.
notes.explanation: The author creates the work product and fixes it.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.3 “Roles and Responsibilities in Reviews”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a tense review meeting, one person calms an argument, keeps the agenda to time and makes sure a junior tester can speak freely. Which role is this?
notes.back: The moderator
notes.choices:
A) The moderator
B) The author
C) The scribe
notes.choicesExplained: B: the author creates and fixes the work product. C: the scribe records; they do not run the meeting.
notes.explanation: Mediation, time management and a safe environment are the moderator’s responsibilities.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.3 “Roles and Responsibilities in Reviews”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Who gathers the anomalies from all reviewers and writes down the decisions made in the review meeting?
notes.back: The scribe
notes.choices:
A) The scribe
B) The review leader
C) The reviewer
notes.choicesExplained: B: the review leader takes overall responsibility and organises the review. C: reviewers find anomalies; they do not collate everyone’s.
notes.explanation: Collating anomalies and recording decisions is the scribe’s job.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.3 “Roles and Responsibilities in Reviews”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A pharmacist who is not on the project is asked to read the drug-interaction rules of a new app and comment. Which review role is she taking?
notes.back: Reviewer
notes.choices:
A) Reviewer
B) Moderator
C) Author
notes.choicesExplained: B: she is not running the meeting. C: she did not create the work product.
notes.explanation: A reviewer performs the review and may be a subject matter expert or other stakeholder.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.3 “Roles and Responsibilities in Reviews”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Who takes overall responsibility for a review, choosing the participants and booking when and where it will happen?
notes.back: The review leader
notes.choices:
A) The review leader
B) The moderator
C) The scribe
notes.choicesExplained: B: the moderator ensures meetings run well but does not own the whole review. C: the scribe records information.
notes.explanation: Overall responsibility and organising people, time and place fall to the review leader.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.3 “Roles and Responsibilities in Reviews”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the difference between the review leader and the moderator?
notes.back: The review leader takes overall responsibility and organises the review; the moderator makes sure the review meetings run effectively.
notes.explanation: Both roles organise, but at different scales: the whole review versus its meetings.
notes.contrast: Owner of the review versus facilitator of its meetings.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.3 “Roles and Responsibilities in Reviews”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two factors that the required formality of a review depends on?
notes.back: Any two of: the SDLC; process maturity; the work product’s criticality and complexity; legal or regulatory requirements; the need for an audit trail.
notes.explanation: The syllabus introduces these with “such as”, so other factors can count too.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.4 “Review Types”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A medical-device maker must show a regulator a documented record of every design review. Which formality factor points it towards formal reviews?
notes.back: Legal or regulatory requirements, and the need for an audit trail.
notes.explanation: Both factors call for a defined process and documented output.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.4 “Review Types”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Can the same work product be reviewed with different review types?
notes.back: Yes. A draft might get a quick informal review, then a more formal one once it matures.
notes.explanation: Formality can rise as the work product matures.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.4 “Review Types”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides the review objectives, what are two factors the choice of review type is based on?
notes.back: Any two of: project needs; available resources; work product type and risks; business domain; company culture.
notes.explanation: Selecting the right type is key to meeting the review objectives, so context matters.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.4 “Review Types”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the main objective of an informal review?
notes.back: Detecting anomalies.
notes.explanation: With no defined process or formal output, its purpose stays simple.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.4 “Review Types”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A developer asks a colleague to look over a short script before lunch; there is no set procedure and nothing is written up. Which review type is this?
notes.back: Informal review
notes.choices:
A) Informal review
B) Inspection
C) Technical review
notes.choicesExplained: B: an inspection is the most formal type and follows the complete process. C: a technical review is led by a moderator with technically qualified reviewers, and is formal.
notes.explanation: No defined process and no formal documented output are the marks of an informal review.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.4 “Review Types”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Who leads a walkthrough?
notes.back: The author.
notes.explanation: The author guides the others through the work product.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.4 “Review Types”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two objectives a walkthrough can serve?
notes.back: Any two of: evaluating quality and building confidence; educating reviewers; gaining consensus; generating ideas; motivating authors to improve; detecting anomalies.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says a walkthrough “can serve many objectives”, listing these among them.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.4 “Review Types”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Must reviewers perform an individual review before a walkthrough?
notes.back: No. They might, but it is not required.
notes.explanation: The author leads everyone through the material in the session itself.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.4 “Review Types”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A new starter’s first week includes a session where the author of the payment module talks the team through its design, answering questions. Which review type is this?
notes.back: Walkthrough
notes.choices:
A) Walkthrough
B) Technical review
C) Inspection
notes.choicesExplained: B: a technical review is led by a moderator, not the author. C: in an inspection the author cannot even be the review leader.
notes.explanation: An author-led session that also educates reviewers fits a walkthrough.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.4 “Review Types”, p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Who performs a technical review, and who leads it?
notes.back: Technically qualified reviewers perform it, and a moderator leads it.
notes.explanation: Technical expertise does the reviewing; a neutral facilitator runs it.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.4 “Review Types”, p. 37
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are the objectives of a technical review?
notes.back: To gain consensus and make decisions on a technical problem, and also to detect anomalies, evaluate quality, generate ideas and help authors improve.
notes.explanation: Decision-making on a technical problem is what sets it apart from the other types.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.4 “Review Types”, p. 37
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Four senior engineers, led by a moderator, meet to agree which of two database designs to adopt for a new system. Which review type is this?
notes.back: Technical review
notes.choices:
A) Technical review
B) Walkthrough
C) Informal review
notes.choicesExplained: B: a walkthrough is led by the author, not a moderator. C: a moderator-led review aimed at a technical decision is not the informal type.
notes.explanation: Technically qualified reviewers, a moderator, and a technical decision to make mark a technical review.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.4 “Review Types”, p. 37
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which review type is the most formal, and what process does it follow?
notes.back: Inspection; it follows the complete generic review process.
notes.explanation: Being the most formal, it uses every activity and task the process describes.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.4 “Review Types”, p. 37
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the main objective of an inspection?
notes.back: To find the maximum number of anomalies.
notes.explanation: Other objectives exist, but finding as many anomalies as possible comes first.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.4 “Review Types”, p. 37
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In inspections, what are the collected metrics used for?
notes.back: Improving the development lifecycle, with the inspection process itself included.
notes.explanation: Measurement makes the process learn from each inspection.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.4 “Review Types”, p. 37
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which two roles can the author not take in an inspection?
notes.back: Review leader and scribe.
notes.explanation: The syllabus states this restriction for inspections specifically.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.4 “Review Types”, p. 37
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: For an inspection of her own interface specification, the author offers to act as scribe. Is that allowed?
notes.back: No; in an inspection the author cannot be scribe or review leader
notes.choices:
A) No; in an inspection the author cannot be scribe or review leader
B) Yes; any participant may be scribe
C) Yes, provided the moderator agrees
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: the syllabus bars the author from the scribe and review leader roles in inspections, with no exception.
notes.explanation: The restriction applies to inspections as the most formal review type.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.4 “Review Types”, p. 37
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A rail-signalling firm reviews code using fixed roles, the full review process, and counts of anomalies per page that feed its process-improvement programme. Which review type is this?
notes.back: Inspection
notes.choices:
A) Inspection
B) Walkthrough
C) Informal review
notes.choicesExplained: B: a walkthrough is author-led and need not follow the full process. C: an informal review has no defined process or documented output.
notes.explanation: Full process, defined roles and metrics used for improvement mark an inspection.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.4 “Review Types”, p. 37
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Who leads a walkthrough, and who leads a technical review?
notes.back: A walkthrough is led by the author; a technical review is led by a moderator.
notes.explanation: The leader shows the purpose: the author presents their work; a moderator steers a decision.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.4 “Review Types”, p. 37
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does an informal review differ from an inspection in process?
notes.back: An informal review follows no defined process and needs no formal output; an inspection follows the complete generic review process.
notes.explanation: They sit at opposite ends of the formality range.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.4 “Review Types”, p. 37
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What main aim sets a technical review apart from an inspection?
notes.back: A technical review aims to gain consensus and make decisions on a technical problem; an inspection’s main objective is finding the most anomalies.
notes.explanation: Both find anomalies, but their headline purposes differ.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.4 “Review Types”, p. 37
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team needs to review a safety-critical control algorithm and find as many anomalies as possible, with measured results. Which review type fits best?
notes.back: Inspection
notes.choices:
A) Inspection
B) Informal review
C) Walkthrough
notes.choicesExplained: B: an informal review has no defined process or formal output. C: a walkthrough serves many objectives, but finding the maximum number of anomalies with metrics is the inspection’s main aim.
notes.explanation: Maximum anomalies and collected metrics are the inspection’s defining features.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.4 “Review Types”, p. 37
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two factors that contribute to successful reviews?
notes.back: Any two of, among others: clear objectives and measurable exit criteria; right review type; small chunks; feedback; preparation time; management support; training.
notes.explanation: The syllabus lists nine factors; these are some of them.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.5 “Success Factors for Reviews”, p. 37
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A review ends in confusion because nobody knew what it was for or when it would count as finished. Which success factor was missing?
notes.back: Defining clear objectives and measurable exit criteria.
notes.explanation: Without a purpose and an end point, participants cannot tell what to look for or when to stop.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.5 “Success Factors for Reviews”, p. 37
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team uses a quick informal review for a contract that a regulator will audit, and the review proves useless as evidence. Which success factor was missed?
notes.back: Choosing the appropriate review type for the objectives, work product, participants and context.
notes.explanation: The type must suit what the review has to achieve.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.5 “Success Factors for Reviews”, p. 37
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Reviewers given a 300-page specification in one go report that they stopped concentrating after the first 40 pages. Which success factor was missed?
notes.back: Performing reviews on small chunks.
notes.explanation: Small chunks keep reviewers from losing concentration.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.5 “Success Factors for Reviews”, p. 37
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Review findings are filed away and never shared with the authors, who keep making the same mistakes. Which success factor is missing?
notes.back: Providing feedback from reviews to stakeholders and authors.
notes.explanation: Feedback is what lets authors improve their product and their activities.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.5 “Success Factors for Reviews”, p. 37
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Participants receive a design document ten minutes before the review meeting starts. Which success factor has been ignored?
notes.back: Providing adequate time to prepare for the review.
notes.explanation: Reviewers need time to study the work product before they can review it well.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.5 “Success Factors for Reviews”, p. 37
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Staff keep being pulled out of reviews by their managers for “more urgent” work. Which success factor is missing?
notes.back: Support from management for the review process.
notes.explanation: The syllabus lists management support among the factors for successful reviews.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.5 “Success Factors for Reviews”, p. 37
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A company wants reviews to become simply “how we work here”, promoting learning and process improvement. Which success factor is this?
notes.back: Making reviews part of the organisation’s culture.
notes.explanation: The syllabus ties this factor to promoting learning and process improvement.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.5 “Success Factors for Reviews”, p. 37
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A newly appointed scribe has never been shown what the role involves and misses half the decisions. Which success factor is missing?
notes.back: Training every participant well enough that each knows how to carry out their role.
notes.explanation: Each role has specific duties that participants must learn.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.5 “Success Factors for Reviews”, p. 37
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Alongside training, management support and small chunks, {{c1::facilitating meetings}} is among the syllabus’s success factors for reviews.
notes.explanation: It sits alongside the moderator’s duty of making review meetings run effectively.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.5 “Success Factors for Reviews”, p. 37
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What must never be an objective of a review?
notes.back: Evaluating the participants.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says “never”, placing this beside the factor of clear objectives.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.5 “Success Factors for Reviews”, p. 37
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A manager proposes counting the anomalies found in each author’s documents and using the totals in annual appraisals. Is that an acceptable review objective?
notes.back: No. A review must never be used to evaluate the people taking part.
notes.explanation: The syllabus rules this out when it describes defining clear review objectives.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 3.2.5 “Success Factors for Reviews”, p. 37
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In version 4.0 of the syllabus, what happened to the section on review techniques?
notes.back: It was removed, together with the learning objective on applying a review technique.
notes.explanation: Review techniques are still named inside individual review, but are no longer taught as a section of their own.
notes.source: ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, Appendix C “Release Notes”, p. 75
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
